title: Non-coding variant effect prediction · Wednesday, November 25

transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Non-coding variant effect prediction, for Wednesday, November 25.
Let's turn to non-coding variant effect prediction, where today's question is what sequence-to-function models can tell us about individual genomes.

First, a bioRxiv preprint from the Demeulemeester lab asks whether one sample is enough to train such a model. Using Fiber-seq and Nanopore direct RNA-seq from a single genome, HG002, they built FiberTron, a twelve million parameter model that reads 524 kilobases.

It predicts methylation, accessibility and transcription at base-pair resolution, with correlations of zero point eight five to zero point nine seven on held-out chromosomes. On dsQTL and eQTL tasks it matches AlphaGenome despite being over ten times smaller.

Because training uses only reference sequence, the sample's own reads stay free to test variant predictions. It recovered 79 percent of allele-specific accessibility variants in a melanoma line, and flagged oncogenic TERT promoter and TAL1 enhancer mutations.

Whether predictions hold up beyond single-nucleotide variants is the subject of a Research Square preprint from the Feng lab. They compared AlphaGenome and Borzoi on 400 pangenome insertions absent from both reference genomes.

The models hardly agreed: a Spearman correlation of minus zero point zero five, with matching signs only about half the time. For single-nucleotide variants it was zero point six three, though the authors call that contrast descriptive.
With only nine loci checkable against expression data, real calibration wasn't possible. The authors recommend reporting coverage, context sensitivity and calibration separately for insertions.
The third paper, from the Dias lab, introduces EMBHER, a method that asks how much expression heritability a model's internal embeddings capture across individuals.
In whole blood, Borzoi's embeddings recovered much of the heritability explained by genotypes, far more than its predictions, while carrying less ancestry information.
Briefly, the Wu lab presents EditFinder, which predicts A-to-I RNA editing sites and suggests nearby variants could change editing at about ten percent of known sites.
The takeaway: these models are becoming useful for single genomes and for populations, but beyond single-nucleotide variants their predictions still need independent checks.
